specStatements.text: Atoms are very small, having a radius of about 1 × 10^-10 metres.
The basic structure of an atom is a positively charged nucleus composed of both protons and neutrons surrounded by negatively charged electrons.
The radius of a nucleus is less than 1/10 000 of the radius of an atom. Most of the mass of an atom is concentrated in the nucleus.

The electrons are arranged at different distances from the nucleus (different energy levels). The electron arrangements may change with the absorption of electromagnetic radiation (move further from the nucleus; a higher energy level) or by the emission of electromagnetic radiation (move closer to the nucleus; a lower energy level).
In an atom the number of electrons is equal to the number of protons in the nucleus. Atoms have no overall electrical charge.
All atoms of a particular element have the same number of protons. The number of protons in an atom of an element is called its atomic number.
The total number of protons and neutrons in an atom is called its mass number.
Atoms can be represented as shown in this example:
Atoms of the same element can have different numbers of neutrons; these atoms are called isotopes of that element.
Atoms turn into positive ions if they lose one or more outer electron (s).
Students should be able to relate differences between isotopes to differences in conventional representations of their identities, charges and masses.
New experimental evidence may lead to a scientific model being changed or replaced.
Before the discovery of the electron, atoms were thought to be tiny spheres that could not be divided.
The discovery of the electron led to the plum pudding model of the atom. The plum pudding model suggested that the atom is a ball of positive charge with negative electrons embedded in it.

The results from the alpha particle scattering experiment led to the conclusion that the mass of an atom was concentrated at the centre (nucleus) and that the nucleus was charged. This nuclear model replaced the plum pudding model.
Niels Bohr adapted the nuclear model by suggesting that electrons orbit the nucleus at specific distances. The theoretical calculations of Bohr agreed with experimental observations.

Later experiments led to the idea that the positive charge of any nucleus could be subdivided into a whole number of smaller particles, each particle having the same amount of positive charge. The name proton was given to these particles.
The experimental work of James Chadwick provided the evidence to show the existence of neutrons within the nucleus. This was about 20 years after the nucleus became an accepted scientific idea.
Students should be able to describe:
• why the new evidence from the scattering experiment led to a change in the atomic model
• the difference between the plum pudding model of the atom and the nuclear model of the atom.
Details of experimental work supporting the Bohr model are not required.
Details of Chadwick’s experimental work are not required.

scopeNotes.statement: Details of experimental work supporting the Bohr model are not required.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Bohr is taken exactly as far as the specification takes him: he adapted the nuclear model by suggesting that electrons orbit the nucleus at specific distances, and his theoretical calculations agreed with experimental observations. No item asks about spectra, spectral lines, apparatus, quantum conditions or any derivation of allowed orbits, and no item requires a student to name or describe an experiment that supported the Bohr model.

scopeNotes.statement: Details of Chadwick's experimental work are not required.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Chadwick appears only as the source of the evidence for neutrons within the nucleus, about 20 years after the nucleus became an accepted idea. No item asks about his apparatus, the beryllium source, paraffin targets, recoil measurements or the reasoning of the experiment itself; the item on Chadwick tests only which particle his work provided evidence for.

concepts.definition: The smallest particle of an element that still behaves as that element. Atoms are very small, having a radius of about 1 x 10^-10 metres.

The tiny positively charged centre of an atom, composed of both protons and neutrons. Its radius is less than 1/10 000 of the radius of the atom, yet most of the mass of the atom is concentrated in it.
A positively charged particle found in the nucleus. Every nucleus of a given element contains the same number of protons.
An uncharged particle found in the nucleus alongside the protons. Changing the number of neutrons gives a different isotope of the same element.
A negatively charged particle arranged at different distances from the nucleus, outside it. In an atom the number of electrons equals the number of protons.
The nucleus is less than one ten-thousandth of the atomic radius, so on a scale drawing of an atom the nucleus would be invisible and the atom is mostly empty space.
One of the different distances from the nucleus at which electrons in an atom are arranged. Electrons further from the nucleus are at higher energy levels.
When an atom absorbs electromagnetic radiation an electron may move further from the nucleus, to a higher energy level.
When an electron moves closer to the nucleus, to a lower energy level, the atom emits electromagnetic radiation.
An atom has no overall electrical charge because the number of negative electrons equals the number of positive protons in the nucleus.
The number of protons in an atom of an element. All atoms of a particular element have the same atomic number.
The total number of protons and neutrons in an atom.
The conventional representation of an atom, with the mass number written above the atomic number to the left of the chemical symbol, for example mass number 23 and atomic number 11 for sodium.
One of two or more atoms of the same element that have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons, and therefore different mass numbers.
An atom that has lost one or more outer electrons, so that protons outnumber electrons and the particle carries a positive charge.
A description or picture used to explain observations. New experimental evidence may lead to a scientific model being changed or replaced.
The idea, held before the discovery of the electron, that atoms were tiny spheres that could not be divided.
The model that followed the discovery of the electron: the atom is a ball of positive charge with negative electrons embedded in it.
The experiment whose results led to the conclusion that the mass of an atom was concentrated at the centre and that the nucleus was charged.
The model in which the mass and the charge of an atom are concentrated in a tiny central nucleus, with electrons outside it. It replaced the plum pudding model.
Niels Bohr's adaptation of the nuclear model, in which electrons orbit the nucleus at specific distances. His theoretical calculations agreed with experimental observations.

Later experiments led to the idea that the positive charge of any nucleus could be subdivided into a whole number of smaller particles, each with the same amount of positive charge; these were named protons.
The experimental work of James Chadwick provided the evidence for neutrons within the nucleus, about 20 years after the nucleus became an accepted scientific idea.

misconceptions.question: How big is the nucleus compared with the whole atom?
misconceptions.correct: The radius of a nucleus is less than 1/10 000 of the radius of an atom, so the atom is almost entirely empty space.
misconceptions.misconception: The nucleus takes up a good fraction of the middle of the atom, perhaps a tenth of its width, so an atom is fairly solid.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Every textbook diagram has to draw the nucleus big enough to see. Students read those pictures as scale drawings.
misconceptions.correction: Scale it up: if an atom were a sports stadium, the nucleus would be a pea on the centre spot. Volume goes as radius cubed, so under 1/10 000 of the radius means under 1/10^12 of the volume.

misconceptions.question: An atom has a radius of about 1 x 10^-10 m. What is 1 x 10^-15 m the size of?
misconceptions.correct: 1 x 10^-15 m is roughly the radius of a nucleus, not of an atom.
misconceptions.misconception: 1 x 10^-15 m is the radius of an atom, because atoms are extremely small.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Two very small powers of ten are learned in the same lesson and students remember the smaller one as the more impressive 'atom' figure.
misconceptions.correction: Anchor the atom first: atom about 1 x 10^-10 m. The nucleus is smaller by a factor of more than 10 000, which lands near 10^-15 m.

misconceptions.question: What is in the nucleus of an atom?
misconceptions.correct: The nucleus is composed of both protons and neutrons; the electrons are outside it.
misconceptions.misconception: The nucleus contains protons and electrons, because opposite charges attract and stick together.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students know the nucleus is where the charge is, and reason that both charged particles must therefore live there.
misconceptions.correction: Only protons and neutrons sit in the nucleus. Electrons are arranged at different distances from the nucleus, outside it.

misconceptions.question: Where is most of an atom's mass?
misconceptions.correct: Most of the mass of an atom is concentrated in the nucleus.
misconceptions.misconception: The electrons carry much of the mass, because an atom has many of them and they fill the whole volume.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Volume is confused with mass: electrons occupy nearly all of the space, so students assume they contribute nearly all of the substance.
misconceptions.correction: Mass and volume are separate. Electrons occupy almost all the volume but almost none of the mass; the protons and neutrons hold it.

misconceptions.question: Is the mass of an atom spread out evenly?
misconceptions.correct: No. Most of the mass of an atom is concentrated in the nucleus at the centre.
misconceptions.misconception: The mass is spread evenly through the sphere of the atom, like the mass of a marble.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Atoms are drawn as filled circles, and everyday solid objects do have evenly spread mass.
misconceptions.correction: The scattering experiment is exactly the evidence against this: an evenly spread atom could not deflect an alpha particle backwards.

misconceptions.question: An electron absorbs electromagnetic radiation. Which way does it move?
misconceptions.correct: It moves further from the nucleus, to a higher energy level.
misconceptions.misconception: It moves closer to the nucleus, because taking in energy pulls it inwards.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Absorb' sounds like being drawn in, and students picture the electron being sucked towards the centre.
misconceptions.correction: Energy in means the electron is lifted away from the attraction of the nucleus: further out is a higher energy level. Emission is the reverse.

misconceptions.question: Does absorbing or emitting radiation remove the electron from the atom?
misconceptions.correct: No. The electron changes energy level; it moves further from or closer to the nucleus but stays in the atom.
misconceptions.misconception: Absorbing radiation throws the electron out of the atom, and emitting radiation is the electron leaving.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Ionisation is met in the same topic, so any electron movement gets read as the electron escaping.
misconceptions.correction: Changing energy level is a move between allowed distances inside the atom. Losing an electron altogether is ionisation, a different event.

misconceptions.question: Can an electron sit at any distance from the nucleus?
misconceptions.correct: No. The electrons are arranged at different distances from the nucleus, at specific energy levels.
misconceptions.misconception: Electrons can orbit anywhere, at any distance, like a satellite in any orbit.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The planetary picture of the atom carries over from gravity, where any orbit radius is possible.
misconceptions.correction: Bohr's contribution was exactly this: electrons orbit at specific distances, and his calculations then agreed with observation.

misconceptions.question: Why does an atom have no overall charge?
misconceptions.correct: Because the number of electrons equals the number of protons, so the charges cancel exactly.
misconceptions.misconception: Because the neutrons in the nucleus cancel out the charge of the protons.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The name 'neutron' sounds like the thing that makes the atom neutral, so students give it that job.
misconceptions.correction: Neutrons have no charge at all, so they cannot cancel anything. Neutrality comes from equal numbers of protons and electrons.

misconceptions.question: How many electrons does a neutral atom have?
misconceptions.correct: The same number as it has protons in its nucleus.
misconceptions.misconception: The same number as it has neutrons, so that the particles balance.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The two words look and sound alike, and both particles are counted from the nuclear symbol.
misconceptions.correction: Match electrons to protons, because those are the two charged particles. Neutron number is mass number minus atomic number.

misconceptions.question: What does the atomic number count?
misconceptions.correct: The number of protons in an atom of that element.
misconceptions.misconception: The number of protons and neutrons added together.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both numbers appear in the same symbol and both are described as 'numbers of particles in the nucleus'.
misconceptions.correction: Atomic number is protons only. Protons plus neutrons is the mass number, the larger figure written above it.

misconceptions.question: Does the atomic number tell you about the outer electrons?
misconceptions.correct: The atomic number is the number of protons; in a neutral atom that equals the total number of electrons, not the outer ones.
misconceptions.misconception: The atomic number is the number of electrons in the outer shell of the atom.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Chemistry lessons stress outer-shell electrons and group number, and the two 'numbers' get merged.
misconceptions.correction: Group number relates to outer electrons; atomic number counts protons, and therefore all the electrons in a neutral atom.

misconceptions.question: What does the mass number count?
misconceptions.correct: The total number of protons and neutrons in an atom.
misconceptions.misconception: Only the neutrons, since the neutrons are what add extra mass.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Isotopes differ in mass number and in neutrons, so students conclude the mass number is a neutron count.
misconceptions.correction: Mass number is protons plus neutrons. Neutron number is what is left after subtracting the atomic number.

misconceptions.question: In the conventional representation, which number goes on top?
misconceptions.correct: The mass number goes on top; the atomic number goes below it.
misconceptions.misconception: The atomic number goes on top, because that is the number the element is listed by.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Periodic table entries vary in layout, and 'atomic' feels like the more important label, so it is put first.
misconceptions.correction: The larger of the two numbers is always the mass number, and it sits above the atomic number. For sodium: 23 above 11.

misconceptions.question: How do you get the number of neutrons from the symbol?
misconceptions.correct: Subtract the atomic number from the mass number.
misconceptions.misconception: Add the two numbers together to find the neutrons.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students remember that the mass number involves combining particles and apply the addition in the wrong direction.
misconceptions.correction: Mass number = protons + neutrons, so neutrons = mass number - atomic number. For sodium, 23 - 11 = 12 neutrons.

misconceptions.question: What is different between two isotopes of an element?
misconceptions.correct: The number of neutrons, and therefore the mass number.
misconceptions.misconception: The number of protons is different, which is why the masses differ.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Any change to the nucleus gets attributed to protons, the particle students think of first.
misconceptions.correction: Change the protons and you change the element. Isotopes of one element must all have the same number of protons.

misconceptions.question: Are isotopes atoms that have gained or lost electrons?
misconceptions.correct: No. Isotopes have different numbers of neutrons; their electron numbers are the same.
misconceptions.misconception: Isotopes are atoms of an element that have gained or lost electrons.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Isotopes and ions are taught together as 'atoms that are not standard', and the two definitions get swapped.
misconceptions.correction: Electrons change gives an ion, with a charge. Neutrons change gives an isotope, with a different mass number and no charge.

misconceptions.question: What kind of ion forms when an atom loses an electron?
misconceptions.correct: A positive ion, because the protons now outnumber the electrons.
misconceptions.misconception: A negative ion, because the atom has lost something, so its charge goes down.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Losing' is read as 'becoming less', and students attach that to the sign of the charge instead of to the negative particles.
misconceptions.correction: Count the charges: remove a negative electron and the positives left over win, so the ion is positive.

misconceptions.question: Can an atom become a positive ion by gaining a proton?
misconceptions.correct: No. Atoms turn into positive ions by losing one or more outer electrons.
misconceptions.misconception: An atom becomes positive when an extra proton joins its nucleus.
misconceptions.whyItArises: It looks like the direct route to a positive charge, and students forget that changing the protons changes the element.
misconceptions.correction: Adding a proton would make a different element altogether. Ion formation only moves outer electrons.

misconceptions.question: Does the mass number change when an atom forms an ion?
misconceptions.correct: No. Losing an electron changes the charge but leaves the mass number unchanged.
misconceptions.misconception: The mass number falls by one for each electron lost.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Any particle leaving seems as though it must reduce the mass, and 'mass number' invites that reasoning.
misconceptions.correction: Mass number counts only protons and neutrons. An electron's mass is negligible and it is not counted, so 23 stays 23.

misconceptions.question: Can an accepted scientific model be replaced?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. New experimental evidence may lead to a scientific model being changed or replaced.
misconceptions.misconception: Once a model is accepted it has been proved, so any result that disagrees with it must be a mistake.
misconceptions.whyItArises: School science is met as settled fact, so 'accepted' is heard as 'proved for good'.
misconceptions.correction: The atom is the standard example: sphere, then plum pudding, then nuclear, then Bohr, each changed by new evidence.

misconceptions.question: What was the atom thought to be before the electron was discovered?
misconceptions.correct: A tiny sphere that could not be divided.
misconceptions.misconception: A tiny sphere with a nucleus already at its centre.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The modern picture is so familiar that students cannot imagine a model without a nucleus in it.
misconceptions.correction: The nucleus only arrived after the scattering experiment, which was years after the electron. Before the electron the atom was indivisible.

misconceptions.question: When did the plum pudding model appear?
misconceptions.correct: After the discovery of the electron, which is what the model was invented to accommodate.
misconceptions.misconception: Before the electron was discovered, as the earliest picture of the atom.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The plum pudding model feels primitive, so it is filed as the very first idea about atoms.
misconceptions.correction: The model needs electrons in it, so it cannot pre-date them. Order: indivisible sphere, then plum pudding, then nuclear.

misconceptions.question: What did the plum pudding model look like?
misconceptions.correct: A ball of positive charge with negative electrons embedded in it.
misconceptions.misconception: A small positive nucleus at the centre with electrons orbiting around it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Only one atomic picture is remembered clearly, and the label is attached to whichever model is described.
misconceptions.correction: Plum pudding has no nucleus at all: the positive charge is spread through the whole ball, with electrons stuck in it.

misconceptions.question: Which model has the electrons embedded in positive charge?
misconceptions.correct: The plum pudding model. In the nuclear model the charge and mass are concentrated in a tiny nucleus.
misconceptions.misconception: The nuclear model, which has electrons sitting inside the ball of positive charge.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The two models are learned as a pair and the descriptions are matched to the wrong names under exam pressure.
misconceptions.correction: Nuclear model: tiny charged centre, electrons outside. Plum pudding: charge spread out, electrons embedded within it.

misconceptions.question: What happened to most alpha particles in the scattering experiment?
misconceptions.correct: Most passed straight through the foil without being deflected.
misconceptions.misconception: Nearly all of them bounced straight back off the foil.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The surprising result is the memorable one, so the rare event is remembered as the usual one.
misconceptions.correction: The evidence has two halves: most passing through shows the atom is mostly empty; a few deflected shows a tiny dense charged centre.

misconceptions.question: Were the alpha particles all deflected in the same way?
misconceptions.correct: No. Most were not deflected at all, and only a small number were deflected through large angles.
misconceptions.misconception: Every alpha particle was deflected by about the same angle as it went through.
misconceptions.whyItArises: A uniform result is what most school experiments give, so students expect consistency here too.
misconceptions.correction: A uniform deflection would suggest evenly spread charge. It is the mixture of outcomes that points to a tiny nucleus.

misconceptions.question: What did Niels Bohr contribute?
misconceptions.correct: He adapted the nuclear model by suggesting that electrons orbit the nucleus at specific distances.
misconceptions.misconception: He proposed the nuclear model itself, by discovering that the atom has a nucleus.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Bohr's name is attached to the familiar orbit diagram, which students take to be the whole nuclear model.
misconceptions.correction: The nucleus came from the scattering experiment. Bohr's addition was the specific allowed distances, which matched calculation.

misconceptions.question: Is the positive charge of a nucleus a single lump?
misconceptions.correct: No. It can be subdivided into a whole number of smaller particles, each with the same amount of positive charge: protons.
misconceptions.misconception: The nuclear charge is one indivisible piece of positive charge that cannot be split up.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The nucleus is drawn as a single blob, and the early nuclear model did treat its charge as one quantity.
misconceptions.correction: Later experiments showed the charge comes in equal whole units. Each unit is a proton, so nuclear charge is a whole number of them.

misconceptions.question: What did James Chadwick's work show?
misconceptions.correct: It provided the evidence for the existence of neutrons within the nucleus.
misconceptions.misconception: It provided the evidence for the nucleus itself, or for the proton.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The three nuclear discoveries are listed together and the names get attached to the wrong particle.
misconceptions.correction: Chadwick's evidence was for the neutron, about 20 years after the nucleus had become an accepted scientific idea.

misconceptions.question: Why was the plum pudding model replaced?
misconceptions.correct: Because new experimental evidence from the scattering experiment could not be explained by it.
misconceptions.misconception: Because the newer picture was simpler and neater to draw and teach.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students know models change, but not that evidence is what forces the change, so they reach for convenience instead.
misconceptions.correction: A model is only replaced when observations defeat it. Alpha particles deflected backwards are impossible in a plum pudding atom.

misconceptions.question: In a model of the atom, which particles carry the negative charge?
misconceptions.correct: The electrons are negative in every model, and whatever they sit in or orbit is positive.
misconceptions.misconception: The main body of the atom is negative and the electrons embedded in it are positive.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The signs are memorised as labels on a picture, and the picture is recalled without them, so the pair gets flipped.
misconceptions.correction: Fix one sign and the rest follows: electrons are always negative, so whatever they sit in, or orbit, must be positive.

misconceptions.question: How small is 'very small' for an atom?
misconceptions.correct: About 1 x 10^-10 m, far too small to be seen with any light microscope.
misconceptions.misconception: About a millimetre, which is the smallest length marked on a ruler.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Very small' is judged against everyday experience, and the smallest length a student can actually point at is a millimetre division.
misconceptions.correction: A millimetre is 1 x 10^-3 m, and about ten million atoms would fit across it. An atom is about 1 x 10^-10 m.

misconceptions.question: Which particles does the mass number count?
misconceptions.correct: Protons and neutrons only.
misconceptions.misconception: Protons and electrons, since those are the two numbers that are equal in an atom.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The atomic number is linked with electrons in a neutral atom, so students carry the proton-electron pairing over to the mass number as well.
misconceptions.correction: Mass number counts only the particles in the nucleus. An electron is about 2000 times lighter than a proton and is not counted.

mcqs.stem: Which of these is closest to the radius of a typical atom?

options.text: About 1 x 10^-10 m, a ten-billionth of a metre
options.rationale: The specification gives the radius of an atom as about 1 x 10^-10 metres.

options.text: About 1 x 10^-15 m, the size of a nucleus
options.rationale: This is the order of a nuclear radius. Students who learn the two small figures together pick the smaller one for the atom.

options.text: About 1 x 10^-6 m, a thousandth of a mm
options.rationale: A micrometre is the scale of a bacterium, ten thousand times too large for an atom.

options.text: About 1 x 10^-3 m, the width of a pin head
options.rationale: A millimetre. Chosen by students who equate 'very small' with the smallest length marked on a school ruler.

mcqs.stem: Which statement describes the basic structure of an atom?

options.text: A positive nucleus of protons and electrons, with neutrons outside
options.rationale: Students who reason that both charged particles must be held together by attraction put the electrons in the nucleus.

options.text: A positive nucleus of protons and neutrons, surrounded by electrons
options.rationale: This is the structure given in the specification: a positively charged nucleus composed of protons and neutrons, surrounded by negatively charged electrons.

options.text: A negative nucleus of protons and neutrons, with electrons outside it
options.rationale: The contents of the nucleus are right but its sign is reversed; the protons inside it make the nucleus positive.

options.text: A core of neutrons only, with protons and electrons around it
options.rationale: This misplaces the protons. It appeals to students who treat the nucleus as the 'neutral middle' of the atom.

mcqs.stem: How does the radius of a nucleus compare with the radius of the atom?

options.text: It is about 1/10 of the atom's radius, as pictured
options.rationale: Taken straight from textbook drawings, where the nucleus has to be drawn large enough to be visible.

options.text: It is roughly 1/100 of the atom's radius in all atoms
options.rationale: A partial correction: the student knows the diagram exaggerates but stops several orders of magnitude too soon.

options.text: It is less than 1/10 000 of the atom's radius
options.rationale: The specification states that the radius of a nucleus is less than 1/10 000 of the radius of an atom.

options.text: It is about half of the atom's whole radius
options.rationale: Treats the atom as essentially solid, with a nucleus filling much of the middle.

mcqs.stem: Where is nearly all of the mass of an atom found?

options.text: In the electrons, because there are so many of them
options.rationale: Confuses volume with mass: electrons fill almost all the space, so students credit them with almost all the substance.

options.text: Spread out evenly throughout the atom's volume
options.rationale: The everyday picture of a solid sphere, which the scattering experiment specifically disproved.

options.text: In the nucleus, which holds the protons only
options.rationale: Right about the location but wrong about the contents; the neutrons contribute about half of the nuclear mass.

options.text: In the nucleus, in the protons and neutrons
options.rationale: Most of the mass of an atom is concentrated in the nucleus.

mcqs.stem: An electron in an atom absorbs electromagnetic radiation. What happens to that electron?

options.text: It moves closer to the nucleus, to a lower energy level
options.rationale: 'Absorb' is read as being drawn inwards, so the direction of the change is reversed.

options.text: It moves further from the nucleus, to a higher energy level
options.rationale: Absorption of electromagnetic radiation moves an electron further from the nucleus, to a higher energy level.

options.text: It escapes the atom, leaving behind a positive ion
options.rationale: Confuses a change of energy level with ionisation, which is a different event met in the same topic.

options.text: It stays where it is but orbits a little quicker
options.rationale: Keeps the energy but refuses to change the arrangement, missing the point that the levels are the store.

mcqs.stem: An atom emits electromagnetic radiation. What has one of its electrons done?

options.text: Moved further from the nucleus, to a higher energy level
options.rationale: The absorption case, applied to emission; the two directions are learned as a pair and swapped.

options.text: Left the atom, carrying the energy away with it
options.rationale: Treats emission as the electron itself departing rather than radiation being given out.

options.text: Moved closer to the nucleus, to a lower energy level
options.rationale: Emission of electromagnetic radiation accompanies an electron moving closer to the nucleus, to a lower energy level.

options.text: Settled at a new distance of its own choosing
options.rationale: Assumes electrons may sit anywhere, ignoring that they occupy specific energy levels.

mcqs.stem: Why does an atom have no overall electrical charge?

options.text: Its neutrons cancel out the charge of the protons
options.rationale: The name 'neutron' is taken to mean the particle that neutralises the atom.

options.text: It has just as many electrons as it has neutrons
options.rationale: The two nuclear particle names are confused, and the wrong pair is matched up.

options.text: Its charges are much too small to be noticed
options.rationale: Dismisses the charges rather than balancing them; small charges still add up to a net charge if they are unequal.

options.text: It has equal numbers of protons and electrons
options.rationale: In an atom the number of electrons is equal to the number of protons, so the charges cancel.

mcqs.stem: What is the atomic number of an element?

options.text: The number of protons in the nucleus
options.rationale: The number of protons in an atom of an element is called its atomic number.

options.text: The number of protons and neutrons added
options.rationale: This is the mass number. Both figures describe nuclear particles, so they are easily interchanged.

options.text: The number of electrons in the outer shell
options.rationale: Imports group number from chemistry, where outer-shell electrons are emphasised.

options.text: The number of neutrons in the nucleus
options.rationale: Picks the other nuclear particle. Neutron number is mass number minus atomic number, not the atomic number itself.

mcqs.stem: What does the mass number of an atom tell you?

options.text: The number of neutrons in the nucleus of the atom
options.rationale: Isotopes differ in both neutrons and mass number, which invites the conclusion that mass number counts neutrons.

options.text: The number of protons and electrons in the atom
options.rationale: Counts the two charged particles instead of the two nuclear ones; electrons are far too light to count.

options.text: The total number of protons and neutrons in the atom
options.rationale: The total number of protons and neutrons in an atom is called its mass number.

options.text: The mass of a single atom, measured in grams
options.rationale: Reads 'mass number' as an actual mass. It is a count of particles and has no unit.

mcqs.stem: An atom of sodium has mass number 23 and atomic number 11. How many neutrons are in its nucleus?

options.text: 11 neutrons, since 11 is the smaller number
options.rationale: Assigns the lower number to the neutrons; the lower number is the atomic number, the protons.

options.text: 34 neutrons, found from 23 + 11 = 34
options.rationale: Adds the two numbers instead of subtracting, a very common slip when the relationship is half remembered.

options.text: 23 neutrons, the larger of the numbers
options.rationale: Reads the mass number itself as the neutron count, forgetting that the protons are included in it.

options.text: 12 neutrons, worked out from 23 - 11 = 12
options.rationale: Mass number = protons + neutrons, so neutrons = 23 - 11 = 12.

mcqs.stem: In the conventional representation of an atom, what does the lower number stand for?

options.text: The atomic number, which counts the protons
options.rationale: The lower number is the atomic number: the number of protons in the atom.

options.text: The mass number, the protons plus the neutrons
options.rationale: Places the mass number underneath. The mass number is the larger figure and is written above.

options.text: The number of neutrons found inside the nucleus
options.rationale: Neither number is a neutron count; neutrons must be worked out by subtraction.

options.text: The charge held by the nucleus in coulombs
options.rationale: Reads the symbol as carrying a measured quantity rather than counts of particles.

mcqs.stem: What are isotopes of an element?

options.text: Atoms which have different numbers of protons
options.rationale: Changing the proton number changes the element, so these could not be isotopes of one element.

options.text: Atoms with equal protons, unequal neutrons
options.rationale: Atoms of the same element can have different numbers of neutrons; these atoms are called isotopes of that element.

options.text: Atoms of the element that have lost an electron
options.rationale: Describes an ion. Isotopes and ions are taught together and their definitions are frequently swapped.

options.text: Atoms of two different elements with the same mass
options.rationale: Equal mass does not make atoms isotopes of each other; isotopes must share the same atomic number.

mcqs.stem: How does an atom turn into a positive ion?

options.text: By gaining one or more electrons from elsewhere
options.rationale: Gaining electrons gives a negative ion; 'gain' is wrongly linked with 'positive'.

options.text: By gaining one extra proton into its nucleus
options.rationale: Would change the element entirely. Ion formation only moves outer electrons.

options.text: By losing one neutron from its own nucleus
options.rationale: Removing an uncharged particle cannot create a charge; it would give a different isotope.

options.text: By losing one or more electrons from its outer shell
options.rationale: Atoms turn into positive ions if they lose one or more outer electrons.

mcqs.stem: Chlorine-35 and chlorine-37 are isotopes. Which statement about them is correct?

options.text: They have the same atomic number but different mass numbers
options.rationale: Isotopes of an element share the proton number and therefore the atomic number, but differ in neutrons and so in mass number.

options.text: They have different atomic numbers and different mass numbers
options.rationale: Attributes the difference to protons, which would make them two different elements.

options.text: They have the same mass number but a different charge
options.rationale: Describes ions of one isotope, and contradicts the labels 35 and 37, which are the mass numbers.

options.text: They have different numbers of electrons in an atom
options.rationale: Neutral atoms of the same element have the same number of electrons whichever isotope they are.

mcqs.stem: A lithium atom with mass number 7 and atomic number 3 loses one electron. What is the resulting ion?

options.text: Charge -1, because one electron has been removed
options.rationale: Links 'losing' with a fall in charge instead of with the removal of a negative particle.

options.text: Charge +1, mass number is still 7, 3 protons
options.rationale: Losing one electron leaves one more proton than electron, so the charge is +1. The nucleus is untouched, so mass number 7 and 3 protons remain.

options.text: Charge +1, mass number 6, with 3 protons still
options.rationale: Correct on charge but reduces the mass number, which counts only protons and neutrons.

options.text: Charge +1, mass number 8, a proton joined
options.rationale: Makes the ion by adding a proton rather than by removing an electron; that would change the element.

mcqs.stem: What should happen to an accepted scientific model when new experimental evidence does not fit it?

options.text: The model is kept, since it is proved
options.rationale: Treats acceptance as proof, so any conflicting result must be discarded instead.

options.text: The evidence is put down to an error
options.rationale: The same error in practical form: the model outranks the observation.

options.text: The model is changed or is replaced
options.rationale: New experimental evidence may lead to a scientific model being changed or replaced.

options.text: The model is kept and the result ignored
options.rationale: Reverses the relationship between evidence and model that the specification is testing here.

mcqs.stem: How were atoms described before the discovery of the electron?

options.text: As tiny spheres that could not be divided at all
options.rationale: Before the discovery of the electron, atoms were thought to be tiny spheres that could not be divided.

options.text: As tiny spheres with a nucleus at their centre
options.rationale: Places the nucleus decades too early; it followed the alpha scattering experiment.

options.text: As balls of positive charge full of electrons
options.rationale: This is the plum pudding model, which could only be proposed once electrons were known.

options.text: As clouds of charge with no definite shape
options.rationale: A modern-sounding picture; the early model was a hard, indivisible sphere.

mcqs.stem: What did the plum pudding model suggest about the atom?

options.text: The atom has a small positive nucleus with electrons orbiting
options.rationale: Describes the nuclear model instead; the two are learned as a pair and the labels get swapped.

options.text: The atom is a ball of positive charge with electrons in it
options.rationale: The plum pudding model suggested that the atom is a ball of positive charge with negative electrons embedded in it.

options.text: The atom is a ball of negative charge with protons in it
options.rationale: Reverses the charges, which is a frequent slip when the picture is recalled without the signs.

options.text: The atom is a solid sphere that cannot be split at all
options.rationale: This is the earlier model, from before the electron was discovered.

mcqs.stem: In the alpha particle scattering experiment, what happened to most of the alpha particles?

options.text: They bounced straight back from the metal foil
options.rationale: The surprising minority result is remembered as the usual one.

options.text: They were deflected by exactly the same angle
options.rationale: Expects the uniform outcome typical of school experiments; the mixture of outcomes is what mattered.

options.text: They passed straight through the metal foil
options.rationale: Most alpha particles passed straight through, which showed that the atom is mostly empty space.

options.text: They were absorbed and stopped in the foil
options.rationale: An absorbing foil would have given no scattering pattern at all to interpret.

mcqs.stem: What is the key difference between the plum pudding model and the nuclear model?

options.text: The nuclear model has the electrons embedded in charge
options.rationale: Swaps the two descriptions; embedded electrons belong to the plum pudding model.

options.text: The plum pudding model has a nucleus at its centre
options.rationale: The plum pudding model has no nucleus; its positive charge fills the whole ball.

options.text: The plum pudding model gave the atom a net charge
options.rationale: Both models describe neutral atoms; the difference is where the charge sits, not how much there is.

options.text: The nuclear model puts the charge at the centre
options.rationale: In the nuclear model the mass of an atom is concentrated at the centre and that nucleus is charged, rather than the charge being spread through the whole atom.

mcqs.stem: What did Niels Bohr add to the nuclear model of the atom?

options.text: Electrons may orbit the nucleus at any distance
options.rationale: Removes exactly the restriction that Bohr introduced, using the planetary analogy instead.

options.text: Electrons orbit the nucleus at specific distances only
options.rationale: Bohr adapted the nuclear model by suggesting that electrons orbit the nucleus at specific distances, and his calculations agreed with observations.

options.text: The nucleus lies at the centre and holds the mass
options.rationale: This was already the nuclear model, established by the scattering experiment before Bohr.

options.text: The nucleus contains neutrons as well as protons
options.rationale: That evidence came later, from Chadwick, and was not part of Bohr's adaptation.

mcqs.stem: Later experiments showed that the positive charge of any nucleus could be subdivided. What followed from this?

options.text: The nuclear charge was shown to be a single indivisible lump
options.rationale: States the opposite of the finding; the point was that the charge divides into equal whole units.

options.text: The neutron was named, a particle carrying no charge
options.rationale: The neutron came later, from Chadwick's work, and carries no charge to subdivide.

options.text: The proton was named, each carrying equal positive charge
options.rationale: The charge was found to be a whole number of equal smaller particles, and the name proton was given to these particles.

options.text: The nucleus itself was shown to be negatively charged
options.rationale: The scattering experiment had already established a positively charged nucleus.

mcqs.stem: What did the experimental work of James Chadwick provide evidence for?

options.text: The existence of a nucleus in every atom
options.rationale: The nucleus was already an accepted idea about 20 years before Chadwick's work.

options.text: The existence of protons inside all atomic nuclei
options.rationale: Protons had been identified earlier, when the nuclear charge was found to subdivide.

options.text: The existence of electron energy levels in atoms
options.rationale: Energy levels belong to Bohr's adaptation of the model, not to Chadwick.

options.text: The existence of neutrons within the nucleus
options.rationale: Chadwick's experimental work provided the evidence to show the existence of neutrons within the nucleus.

mcqs.stem: Why did the scattering experiment lead scientists to change the model of the atom?

options.text: A few alpha particles bounced back, which the old model forbade
options.rationale: A ball of evenly spread positive charge could not repel a fast alpha particle backwards, so the evidence forced a new model with a tiny, dense, charged nucleus.

options.text: Scientists preferred the newer picture because it was simpler to draw
options.rationale: Models are replaced by evidence, not by taste; the nuclear model is in fact harder to picture.

options.text: Every alpha particle bounced back, showing the atom is solid all through
options.rationale: Most passed straight through, which is the half of the evidence showing the atom is mostly empty.

options.text: Nearly all the alpha particles bounced straight back off the foil
options.rationale: Incorrect: only a small fraction bounced back; nearly all passed straight through the foil.
